definition.text: Russian geologist and geographer (1846–1903) credited with laying the foundations of soil science.

facts.text: He is commonly called the father of soil science and was perhaps the first to investigate different soil types across broad geographic areas.
He showed that besides parent material, climate, topography and the length of soil formation explain how soil types vary from place to place.
He saw soil as a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock that becomes soil under climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age.
Building on these ideas, he produced the very first soil classification, which described five factors of soil formation.
He reached his theory after extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883; his most famous work is Russian Chernozem (1883).
His research brought Russian terms such as chernozem, podsol, gley and solonets into the international vocabulary of soil science.
From 1869 to 1901 he published 285 works, including 61 books and 4 maps.
His ideas were taken up by many soil scientists, including Hans Jenny, and the IUSS's Dokuchaev Award, likened to a Nobel Prize for soil science, honours him.

title: Russian Chernozem

definition.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1883 book, his most famous work, a complete study of the chernozem soils of European Russia.

facts.text: It came out of his extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883, from which he arrived at his theory of soil formation.
Studying the steppe soils of the Poltava region, he found that peasants named all soils by colour, and he began to use such names himself.
An English translation by N. Kaner was published in Jerusalem in 1967 for the USDA and NSF.

notes: No article of its own; passes the two-page test (Vasily Dokuchaev, Chernozem § Distribution and § Theories of chernozem origin).

definition.text: German lawyer and land tax assessor (1794–1877) considered one of the founders of modern soil science.

facts.text: Evaluating forest and farmland for Saxony for most of his career, he grew concerned about declining soil quality and related soil profiles to their formation.
In 1862 he argued that soil was separate in nature from geology and introduced the term pedology to found soil study as an independent science.
His First Principles of Soil Science (1857) and Pedology or General and Special Soil Science (1862) turned his field observations into a systematic approach.
The 1862 book proposed a way to describe soil profiles, discussed soils' physical and chemical properties and classified soils by their mineral properties.
He separated pedology, a natural description of soil regardless of plants or use, from agrology, the study of soil in relation to plants and farming.
Dokuchaev proved more influential, but Glinka regarded Fallou as the founder of modern soil science, and Yarilov's 1904 article called him "Founder of Soil Science".

definition.text: German chemist (1803–1873), a principal founder of organic chemistry, who made major contributions to agricultural and biological chemistry.

facts.text: He is called the "father of the fertilizer industry" for stressing nitrogen and minerals as essential plant nutrients and for popularizing the law of the minimum.

His 1840 book Organic Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology argued that chemistry could revolutionize farming; it was widely translated, fiercely criticized and highly influential.
The early concept of soil as a store of plant nutrients rested on his ideas, refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories and field plots.
Around 1840 he suggested dissolving animal bones in sulphuric acid to make fertilizer, a process first used in Britain in 1841.
Seeing both synthesis and decay in living systems made him an early advocate of conservation, including recycling sewage.
Despite criticism of his inexperience in practice, his writings spurred agricultural experiment and debate in Germany, England and France.

definition.text: The theory, synthesized and promoted by Liebig, that plants draw essential nutrients as inorganic minerals from the soil, and carbon and hydrogen from air and water.

facts.text: It opposed the humus theory, which held that decayed plant matter was plants' main carbon source and that fertilizers worked by breaking humus down.
De Saussure's experiments of 1804 suggested plants took carbon from the air and that their mineral content reflected the soil they grew in.
Using more precise measurements, Liebig showed that the humus in a soil could not supply enough carbon for the plants growing on it.
By the late 1830s Karl Sprengel had used Liebig's combustion analysis to show that manures owed their value to their minerals.
Liebig named nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as essential to plant growth, and held that inorganic materials could feed plants as well as organic ones.
He also popularized Sprengel's law of the minimum: growth is limited by the scarcest essential resource, not by the total available.

title: Liebig's nitrogen debate

definition.text: The long dispute over Liebig's claim that plants feed on nitrogen compounds from the air, and over whether crops need nitrogen fertilizer.

facts.text: The claim was contested for many years and turned out true for legumes but not for other plants.
The 1840 and 1842 editions of his book said the air held too little nitrogen and that nitrogen fertilizer, perhaps as ammonia, was needed.
He later decided ammonia in rain supplied enough and argued for years against nitrogen fertilizer; his own nitrogen-poor fertilizer had no appreciable effect in a field test.
By the seventh German edition he admitted mistakes and again called nitrogen fertilizer beneficial or even necessary; in 1863 he came to appreciate biological nitrogen fixation.

contested_note: Whether plants take their nitrogen from the air was disputed for many years; it proved true only for legumes.

definition.text: German-American expert on pedology (1833–1916), considered the father of modern soil science in the United States.

facts.text: He was an authority on climate as a soil-forming factor, on soil chemistry and on the reclamation of alkali soils.
In 1860, in Mississippi, he studied how rock material, climate and vegetation relate to the type of soil that develops.
From 1875 to 1904 he was professor of agricultural chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley, and directed the state agricultural experiment station.
For the Northern Transcontinental Survey of 1881–1883 he studied soils of the southwestern states and Pacific slope in relation to geology, composition, native flora and farming.
His 1892 Relations of Climate to Soils won the Liebig medal in 1894; with his 1906 book Soils it established climate as a soil-forming factor in US thinking.
He and Hopkins greatly influenced Marbut's shift from seeing soils as reflections of geology to treating soil science as a distinct field.

title: Konstantin Glinka

definition.text: Russian soil scientist (1867–1927), a student of Dokuchaev who carried the Russian school's ideas to the wider world.

facts.text: From 1889 he did geological and soil research under Dokuchaev, including work in Poltava and on the Forest Department expedition.
He was the first director of the Dokuchaev Soil Science Institute and wrote over 150 works on soil, geography, mineralogy and geology.
His 1908 soil science textbook included the first schematic soil map of the world.
Language barriers kept the Russian team's work from Western Europe until his German publication of 1914; Marbut translated a version from German into English.
By the 1920s he had found Russian soils that did not fit present climates and were seen as relics of warmer past climates.
In 1927 he became the first soil scientist elected to the USSR Academy of Sciences and led the Soviet delegation to the First International Congress of Soil Scientists in Washington.

conflicts.text: Glinka published the first world soil map in 1906.
conflicts.note: The lead gives 1906; the Career section dates the first schematic world soil map to his 1908 textbook.

notes: S:79bfb62463bf places the 1930 Second International Congress in Moscow, while World Congress of Soil Science (S:d15fc2a1a243) lists Leningrad; not used in facts.

definition.text: American soil scientist (1863–1935) who directed the Soil Survey Division of the US Department of Agriculture from 1913 until his death.

facts.text: He developed the first formal soil classification scheme for the United States, beginning the work in 1920.
Trained as a geologist and geographer, he first saw soils as surface reflections of the geology beneath but came to see soil science as distinct from geology.
In 1927 he translated Glinka's The Great Soil Groups of the World and their Development into English and applied the Russian ideas to a national classification.
His scheme became the 1935 system, modified and published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture as the 1938 USDA soil taxonomy.
At its highest level it divided soils into pedocals, carbonate-rich soils of drier climates, and pedalfers, rich in aluminium and iron; "alfer" became the root of alfisol.
He died of pneumonia in 1935 on his way to advise the Chinese Geological Survey on organizing a soil survey.

definition.text: Swiss-born soil scientist (1899–1992) and expert in pedology, above all in the processes of soil formation.

facts.text: He took a doctorate at ETH Zurich in 1927 on ion exchange reactions and joined the University of California, Berkeley, in 1936.
International recognition followed his 1941 book Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology.
It combined field studies with the formalism of physical chemistry to relate soil properties to climate, biota, relief, parent material and time, leaving room for further variables.
In The Soil Resource, Origin and Behaviour (1980) he recast the factors as state variables and extended their effects to ecosystem properties.
His factors underlie the CLORPT model of soil-landscape modelling and, adapted for description rather than explanation, the scorpan approach of digital soil mapping.
He studied the Mendocino pygmy forest, whose stunted plants grow on a 500,000-year-old marine terrace; a reserve there bears his name.
In his 1980 article "Alcohol or Humus" he argued against turning crop residues and forest humus into fuel, which would curtail carbon and nitrogen cycles and speed humus oxidation.
He was President of the Soil Science Society of America in 1949.

definition.text: Swedish chemist and agricultural scientist (1846–1916) who created the Atterberg limits still used by geotechnical engineers.

facts.text: Around the age of fifty-four he turned to the classification and plasticity of soils, the work he is most remembered for.
He proposed the first texture classification, the international system, in 1905, and was apparently the first to set 0.002 mm as the upper size of clay particles.
Finding plasticity characteristic of clay, he devised in 1911 the consistency limits named after him; Terzaghi brought them into geotechnics and Casagrande standardized the tests in 1932.
The International Society of Soil Science formally recognized his soil classification work at Berlin in 1913, and his grain size scale is still the one used in Sweden.

definition.text: Danish forester and naturalist (1840–1926) whose studies of forest soils laid early foundations for the study of humus forms.

facts.text: His seminal work on Danish forest soils described mor humus for the first time, calling it beech peat by analogy with sphagnum peat.
His Studies on Forest Soil appeared as a series in 1878–84 in the journal he founded in 1875, the first independent Danish forestry journal, and was translated into German and French.
These studies showed how plant communities and their animals shape the ground surface, as in heathland formation and soil change beneath surface peat.
His last major work, in 1924, concluded that the Danish heaths continue the tundra that arose after the ice age and were never forested like nearby land.

definition.text: Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist, ecologist and soil scientist (1856–1953) who pioneered the cycle-of-life concept.

facts.text: He discovered several biogeochemical cycles and parts of them, and was among the first to study microbes outside medicine, making him an early student of microbial ecology.
In 1887 he found that Beggiatoa oxidizes hydrogen sulfide as an energy source, the first known form of lithotrophy.
From 1888 in Zürich he identified Nitrosomonas and Nitrosococcus, which oxidize ammonium to nitrite, and Nitrobacter, which oxidizes nitrite to nitrate; he described this two-step process in 1890.
He identified Clostridium pasteurianum, a free-living anaerobe that fixes atmospheric nitrogen without living in legume root nodules.
From 1922 he led the Pasteur Institute's agricultural bacteriology division, studying iron and nitrifying bacteria, Azotobacter, cellulose decomposers and culture methods for soil microbes.
His student Vasily Omelianski spread his concepts and methods in the Soviet Union in the following decades.

definition.text: Winogradsky's discovery of chemoautotrophy, popularly called chemosynthesis: organisms drawing energy from inorganic compounds and carbon from carbon dioxide.

facts.text: Until then, autotrophs were believed to get their energy only from light.
Organisms that oxidize hydrogen sulfide or ammonium for energy split autotrophs into photoautotrophs and chemoautotrophs.
His 1887 Beggiatoa work gave the first example of lithotrophy but not autotrophy; his nitrifying bacteria gave the first chemoautotrophy, fixing carbon dioxide into organic compounds.
This form of metabolism is believed to occur only in prokaryotes.

definition.text: Dutch microbiologist and botanist (1851–1931), one of the founders of virology and environmental microbiology.

facts.text: He investigated nitrogen fixation, revealing the symbiosis between legumes and the nodule bacteria that fix nitrogen, a reaction vital to soil fertility and agriculture.
He fully described the fixation process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth, and in 1901 showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
He discovered bacterial sulfate reduction, in which bacteria use sulfate instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, a finding important for understanding biogeochemical cycles.
He isolated Spirillum desulfuricans, now Desulfovibrio desulfuricans, the first known sulfate-reducing bacterium.
He invented the enrichment culture, a fundamental method for studying microbes from the environment.
In 1898 his filtration experiments showed that tobacco mosaic disease is caused by an agent smaller than a bacterium, which he named a virus.
He founded the Delft School of Microbiology; the maxim "everything is everywhere, but the environment selects", often credited to him, was Lourens Baas Becking's.

title: Enrichment culture

definition.text: A fundamental method of culturing microbes taken from the environment so that they can be studied.

facts.text: Martinus Beijerinck invented it; with the discovery of viruses it was one of his two major contributions to microbiology.
Early nitrification researchers, among them Warington, Winogradsky and the Franklands, could at first only enrich cultures of nitrifiers rather than isolate them pure.
Seven of the ten described anammox species are available in laboratory enrichment cultures.

notes: No article crawled; passes the two-page test (Martinus Beijerinck, Microbial ecology, Microorganism, Nitrification, Anammox).

title: Selman Waksman

definition.text: Russian-born American biochemist and microbiologist (1888–1973) whose research on the decomposition of soil organisms enabled the discovery of streptomycin and other antibiotics.

facts.text: As a graduate student he researched soil bacteriology at the New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station and studied soil fungi at the USDA.
He wrote Principles of Soil Microbiology (1927) and Humus (1936); his classical view of humus as distinct from decomposing organic matter long featured in soil science textbooks.
His lignin theory of 1932 is one of three main historical theories of how humic substances form.
His Rutgers team found several antibiotics, including actinomycin, streptomycin and neomycin, and he introduced the modern sense of the word antibiotic.
Streptomycin, from Streptomyces griseus and isolated by his student Albert Schatz, was the first antibiotic used to cure tuberculosis.
He won the 1952 Nobel Prize for systematic studies of soil microbes that led to streptomycin; Schatz contested the credit in 1950 litigation and was recognized as co-discoverer.

contested_note: Credit for discovering streptomycin was disputed between Waksman and his student Albert Schatz, who won recognition as co-discoverer.

definition.text: Pioneer of soil conservation in the United States (1881–1960) and head of the federal soil erosion agency now called the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

facts.text: Working as a soil surveyor from 1903, he came to see soil erosion as a serious problem for the planet, first linking soil quality and erosion in a 1905 Virginia survey.
He co-wrote the USDA's Soil Erosion: A National Menace (1928), his most influential work, against colleagues who held soil to be a resource that cannot be exhausted.
Congressman James P. Buchanan then secured funds in 1929 for erosion studies and a 1930 amendment creating USDA soil erosion experiment stations, whose sites Bennett chose.
He directed the Soil Erosion Service from September 1933; his Dust Bowl advocacy helped pass the act of 27 April 1935 creating the Soil Conservation Service, which he led until 1951.
In the hardest-hit Dust Bowl region, nearly 40,000 farmers had put 5.5 million acres under terraced and contour-listed cultivation by May 1936.
The Coon Creek Watershed Project in Wisconsin was the first of many watershed projects set up to show farmers soil conservation practices.
Creating the Soil Conservation Service marked the US government's acceptance of interpreting soils for soil and water conservation.
He was also instrumental in forming the Soil Conservation Society of America, now the Soil and Water Conservation Society.

conflicts.text: The Soil Erosion Service was established in August 1933 under Bennett.
conflicts.note: Dust Bowl § Government response gives August 1933; the Bennett page gives September 1933.

definition.text: American agricultural scientist (1848–1911) who has been called the father of soil physics in the United States.

facts.text: As professor of agricultural physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison from 1888 to 1902 he applied physics to agriculture, and his greatest impact was on soil science.
He studied soils' water-holding capacity, plants' moisture needs, aeration, the movement of soil water and groundwater and the draft of ploughs, and began studies of soil fertility.
At the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902, he found nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yields, undermining the views of bureau chief Milton Whitney; he was forced to resign.
He is best remembered for Farmers of Forty Centuries, an account of traditional Asian farming now regarded as an organic farming classic.

title: Farmers of Forty Centuries

definition.text: Franklin Hiram King's book on the long-sustained traditional farming of China, Korea and Japan, now regarded as a classic of organic farming.

facts.text: It recounts his nine-month tour of Asia in 1909, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture.
It discussed the advantages of sustainable agriculture and warned that such practices would be vital to farming in the future.
His wife Carrie Baker King finished the last chapter after his death and published the book in 1911.
Lord Northbourne called it a "classic" that no student of farming or social science can afford to ignore.

conflicts.text: King discussed sustainable agriculture in Farmers of Forty Centuries in 1907.
conflicts.note: Sustainable agriculture § History gives 1907; the King page dates the tour to 1909 and publication to 1911.

notes: No article crawled; passes the two-page test (Franklin Hiram King, Sustainable agriculture § History).

definition.text: American agricultural chemist (1866–1919) at the University of Illinois, noted for his research and writing on Illinois soils.

facts.text: From 1894 until his death in 1919 he was chemist at the University of Illinois Agriculture Experiment Station, latterly heading its Department of Agronomy.
With Hilgard, he greatly influenced Marbut's change from seeing soils as reflections of geology to recognizing soil science as distinct from geology.
In 1896 he began the Illinois long-term selection experiment.

definition.text: American soil physicist (1904–1993), one of the most influential figures in 20th-century soil physics.

facts.text: His 1931 Cornell thesis on capillary conduction through porous media made the first decisive advance beyond Buckingham in extending Darcy's law to unsaturated soils.
In it he set out the partial differential equation now called the Richards equation, though Lewis Richardson had published it in 1922.
He described the principles, construction and operation of the tensiometer and proposed the tension plate apparatus for measuring capillary potential in soil.
In 1941 he described the pressure-membrane apparatus, mainly for extracting soil solution for salinity analysis.
Working at the USDA Salinity Laboratory, he and colleagues fixed the accepted limits for plant growth: field capacity at −1/3 bar (−33 J/kg) and permanent wilting point at −15 bar (−1500 J/kg).
He remarked that the concept of available water is oversimplified.
His apparatus and methods moved the study of soil water from a qualitative stage to one based on measurement and mathematics.

definition.text: American soil scientist (1907–1981) who originally developed the USDA soil classification system, Soil Taxonomy.

facts.text: After wartime service he joined the USDA, working from 1946 as a soil correlator for the Soil Conservation Service and from 1952 as Director of Soil Survey Investigations.
Tasked with developing a way to classify soils, he produced the first of seven iterations of what became a system used worldwide.
He developed Soil Taxonomy in collaboration with European soil scientists.
More than 15 years of his work led to the system made official in 1965 and published in 1975.
After retiring in 1973 he advised international partners on applying Soil Taxonomy, and he died in 1981 in Ghent, where he taught.

definition.text: American soil scientist (1908–2008) who studied soils across the United States and on islands of the Western Pacific.

facts.text: Trained under Charles E. Kellogg and Emil Truog, he joined the USDA soil survey programmes after teaching at Iowa State College.
During World War II he mapped soils on Western Pacific islands for the Military Geology Unit.
He was the soil survey's Director for Soil Classification and Correlation from 1953 to 1971.
He became editor-in-chief of the journal Geoderma in 1967 and wrote a history of US soil survey and classification from 1899 to 1970.

definition.text: Indian-American soil scientist (born 1944), a pioneer of soil-centred farm management for food security and climate-resilient agriculture.

facts.text: Working in Nigeria from 1970 to 1987, he found organic carbon and nutrients disappeared after deforestation, and studied mulching, cover crops and no-till farming to restore them.
His most cited paper, in Science in 2004, was the first report that restoring soil organic matter both improves soil health and lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Departing from the 1970s reliance on commercial fertilizer, his work showed how no-till, cover crops, residues, mulching and agroforestry rebuild degraded soils and sequester carbon.
His models suggest that restoring soil health could by 2100 double global grain yield, cut the land used for grain by 30% and reduce fertilizer use.
He founded the Rattan Lal Center for Carbon Management and Sequestration at Ohio State and launched the C-FARM carbon farming project in 2021.
He was IUSS president in 2017–2018 and won the Japan Prize in 2019 and the World Food Prize in 2020.

definition.text: German botanist and agricultural scientist (1787–1859) who first stated the law of the minimum.

facts.text: He trained in agriculture under Albrecht Thaer and then with Heinrich Einhof at Möglin from 1804 to 1808.
He studied natural sciences at Göttingen from 1821 to 1828 and became a professor there.
He was the first to state the 'theory of minimum' in agricultural chemistry: plant growth is limited by the essential nutrient present at the lowest concentration.
The rule is often credited to Justus von Liebig as Liebig's law of the minimum, but Liebig only popularised it later.
He founded the Academy of Agriculture at Regenwalde (Resko), where he taught and researched until his death in 1859.
His books include an 1839 study of manures and their action and the 1844 Die Bodenkunde, with a full guide to the chemical analysis of field soils.

title: Jean-Baptiste Boussingault

definition.text: French chemist (1801–1887) who made major contributions to agricultural science.

facts.text: From 1836 he worked mainly on agricultural chemistry and plant and animal physiology.
In 1836 he set up the first agricultural experiment station on his wife's estate at Pechelbronn in Alsace, some seven years before Rothamsted.
He revived the quantitative methods first used by de Saussure and is called the father of field plot technique.
He made the first analysis of crops grown in a rotation and showed that soil nitrogen rises after legume crops.
He found plant growth proportional to the available nitrogen, so applying phosphorus and nitrogen together gives greater growth.
He asked whether plants can take up free nitrogen from the air; he answered no, laying a basis for what became the nitrogen cycle.
In 1839 he was given the chair of agricultural and analytical chemistry at the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers in Paris.
Liebig hailed him as a pioneer of soil and plant chemistry, and his work on nitrogen in plant growth prepared the way for nitrogen fertilizers.

notes: nutrient-cycles drafts cite a source saying he discovered biological nitrogen fixation in 1838; this page (S:c8f6c6db90c3) says he answered the free-nitrogen question in the negative. Verification pass should compare.

definition.text: English entrepreneur and agricultural scientist (1814–1900) who founded the experimental farm that became Rothamsted Research.

facts.text: Before leaving Oxford in 1832 he began testing manures on plants in pots at Rothamsted, soon extending the trials to field crops.
In 1842 he patented a manure made by treating phosphates with sulphuric acid, a superphosphate that began the artificial fertilizer industry.
From the following year he worked with Joseph Henry Gilbert for more than half a century on crop and animal-feeding experiments.
He and Gilbert jointly received the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1867.
In 1889 he endowed the Lawes Agricultural Trust to keep the experimental farm going; Rothamsted is the oldest agricultural research facility in the world.

definition.text: German agronomist and microbiologist (1862–1923) who developed the concept of the rhizosphere and helped found microbial ecology.

facts.text: At the Tharandt research station he studied the symbiosis of legumes with root-nodule bacteria, work that produced the first cultures of rhizobium bacteria.
He also showed the importance of root nodules for the nitrogen nutrition of black alder.
In 1893 he and F. Nobbe published 'Inoculate the Soil!'.
In an April 1904 lecture he introduced the term rhizosphere for the soil directly affected by root secretions and their microorganisms.

definition.text: German botanist, plant pathologist and mycologist (1839–1900) who coined the term mycorrhiza.

facts.text: He named the mycorrhiza in an 1885 paper on the root-symbiosis nutrition of certain trees by underground fungi.
A failed royal commission to develop truffle cultivation led him to work out the nature and development of mycorrhizae.
In 1877 he coined the term symbiosis to describe lichens.
The bacterial genus Frankia is named after him.

definition.text: German agronomist (1752–1828) and supporter of the humus theory of plant nutrition.

facts.text: A physician by training, he turned from flower gardening to agriculture and became known across Europe for applying science to farming practice.
He is described as the first agricultural scientist to arrange the existing facts and theory of agriculture into a proper system.
In 1802 he founded the first German agricultural training institute at Celle, where he experimented with crop rotation to raise yields.
In 1804 he founded the first German agricultural academy at Möglin, renamed the Royal Prussian Academy of Agriculture in 1819.
His academy analysed many soils and classified specimens by their dominant components, such as sand, lime or red and blue clay, marking each with coloured labels.
Thaer's soil classification came into common use on large German estates.
His four-volume Grundsätze der rationellen Landwirthschaft (1809–1812), covering the theory of soil, ploughing, manuring and irrigation, appeared in English in 1844 as The Principles of Agriculture.
The humus theory set out in that work was still accepted in the period 1800–1860.

title: Charles Darwin

definition.text: English naturalist, geologist and biologist (1809–1882), best known for his contributions to evolutionary biology.

facts.text: His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836 established him as an eminent geologist.

When shown ground where cinders had vanished under loam, he suggested earthworms were responsible, a theory of their role in soil formation that he presented to the Geological Society on 1 November 1837.
His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881), counted among his works of great importance.

notes: General biography page; drafted only from its soil and earthworm sentences.

definition.text: American physicist (1867–1940) who worked as a soil physicist at the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 to 1906.

facts.text: His first soil physics work was on soil aeration: the loss of carbon dioxide from soil and its replacement by oxygen.

He found the rate of gas diffusion in soil did not depend much on structure, compactness or water content, and gave the diffusion coefficient as an empirical function of air content, a relation still cited in textbooks.
He concluded that soil gas exchange takes place by diffusion and is largely independent of changes in outside barometric pressure.
His soil water work appeared in 1907 as Bulletin 38 of the USDA Bureau of Soils, Studies on the movement of soil moisture.
He showed that soils can strongly inhibit evaporation, especially where capillary flow through the uppermost layers is cut off.
Arid soils first lost more water than humid ones but then less, which he put down to the soil forming a natural mulch.
He named the capillary potential arising from soil–water interactions, now called the matric or water potential.
He was the first to set out how hydraulic conductivity depends on capillary potential, and applied a formula equivalent to Darcy's law to unsaturated flow.

title: Edmund Ruffin

definition.text: American planter, politician and scientist (1794–1865), known for pioneering methods to preserve and improve soil productivity.

facts.text: He is best known as an early advocate of secession of the Southern slave states, and farmed his plantations with enslaved labour.
In his twenties he began experimenting with marl to rejuvenate land worn out by more than a century of tobacco monoculture.
He recommended crop rotation and amendments for exhausted soils, and studied bogs and swamps to learn how to correct soil acidity.
He experimented with lime to raise the pH of peat soils.
His book An Essay on Calcareous Manures explained how calcareous earths (marl) had cut soil acidity and raised corn and wheat yields.
His advice to use marl was not widely followed in his own time, but he has since been called the father of soil science in the United States.

notes: Soil-science facts only; the political career is summarized in one fact for context.

definition.text: American pedologist, educator and musician (1913–2002), known for mapping Wisconsin's soils and for popularizing soil science.

facts.text: He created the periodical Soil Survey Horizons in 1960 and co-created the Soils of Wisconsin Map published in 1968.
He co-authored the textbook Soil Genesis and Classification with Stanley Buol and Ralph McCracken, first published in 1973 and used in courses worldwide.
His Soils of Wisconsin (1976) explained soil development following Hans Jenny's factors of soil formation and divided the state into regions A to J.
He campaigned for Antigo silt loam, which the Wisconsin legislature named the official state soil in 1983.

definition.text: English chemist (1817–1901) who spent a long career improving the methods of practical agriculture.

facts.text: A former doctoral student of Justus von Liebig at Giessen, he became director of the chemical laboratory at Lawes's Rothamsted experiment station in 1843.
He worked there from June 1843 until his death, and conducted most of the meticulous studies published under both names.
In 1843 Lawes and Gilbert began long-term field experiments at Rothamsted, some still running.
They found that cereal crops take up nitrogen from the soil, contrary to Liebig's view that it came only from the air.
Their work made Rothamsted a leading centre of agricultural research.

definition.text: Russian soil scientist (1872–1932) of Lithuanian origin, founder of colloidal soil chemistry in Russia.

facts.text: He introduced the concept of the soil absorbing complex and distinguished mechanical, physico-chemical and biological types of soil absorption capacity.
He classified soils by composition, separating soils unsaturated with cations from those saturated with calcium or with sodium ions.
He explained the evolution of saline soils chemically and laid the theoretical basis of liming and of adding gypsum to soil.
He led the chemistry laboratory of the Dokuchaev Soil Institute (1915–17) and headed the institute in 1929–30.
He was president of the International Union of Soil Sciences from 1927 to 1930 and received the Lenin Prize in 1927.

definition.text: Swiss chemist and plant physiologist (1767–1845), a major pioneer in the study of photosynthesis.

facts.text: He studied plant gas exchange and how different soils affected plant growth, work gathered in Recherches chimiques sur la Végétation (1804).
He based his conclusions on extensive quantitative data, unlike some predecessors.
He showed plants take their carbon from atmospheric carbon dioxide, not from soil humus as most of his immediate predecessors believed.
He showed plants need mineral nutrients taken up from the soil, disproving the idea that plant minerals arose by transmutation inside the plant.
His findings were largely neglected for decades until Liebig revived them and Boussingault's field research confirmed the importance of soil mineral nutrients.
Liebig used de Saussure's results to critique humus theories.

definition.text: American soil scientist (1869–1938) who wrote on the nitrogen cycle.

facts.text: He headed the department of soil technology at the Cornell University College of Agriculture from 1912.
At Cornell's Caldwell Field he ran many field studies, including lysimeter and plot experiments.
In 1913 he and James A. Bizzell won the Howard N. Potts Medal for a paper on how certain non-leguminous plants relate to soil nitrate content.
From 1907 he published soil science textbooks; his Principles of Soil Management went through 10 editions.

title: Milton Whitney

definition.text: The first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, forerunner of the federal soil survey.

facts.text: Franklin Hiram King's finding that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yield undermined Whitney's firmly held views on soil chemistry and fertility.
George Nelson Coffey's map was not released as an official Bureau map because it did not fit Whitney's prevailing soil classification concepts.

title: Nikolai Sibirtsev

definition.text: Russian soil scientist (1860–1900) who led the Russian school of soil science with Dokuchaev.

facts.text: From 1870 the school under Dokuchaev and Sibirtsev developed a new concept of soil.
He taught soil science as a professor; Konstantin Glinka took over his teaching when he fell ill.
He is also counted among the Russian geographers who made great contributions to physical geography.

title: Heath

definition.text: A shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining, infertile, acidic soils, with open, low-growing woody vegetation.

facts.text: Heathland is favoured by hard, dry climates, especially in summer, and by acidic, low-fertility, often sandy and free-draining soils; a small mire may form where drainage is poor.
Heaths are dominated by low shrubs 20 cm to 2 m tall and range from very species-rich in Australia and South African fynbos to depauperate in Europe, where heather, heath and gorse dominate.

Many heaths are anthropogenic, made by centuries of clearing woodland by grazing and burning, and are kept by grazing and periodic burning (swailing) or rarely mowing, or they are recolonised by woodland.
Heaths are widespread but rapidly disappearing and rare in Europe; tree incursion after traditional management stopped and urban sprawl threaten them.
